## Chapultepec in Mexico City: park, castle, and museums

**Chapultepec (Bosque de Chapultepec)** is an extensive green space in [Mexico City](/mexico/place/mexico-city-and-teotihuacan/). Travelers know the name for its park, hilltop castle, and several major museums. Unlike the historic center around the [Zócalo](/mexico/place/mexico-city-zocalo/), this area reveals the city through landscapes and exhibition spaces.

In Chapultepec, you can stroll along tree-lined paths, enjoy lake views, and devote part of the day to cultural attractions. But the park is too large to explore every site thoroughly in a few hours. For a first visit, decide in advance whether nature, history, or museum collections interest you most.

## Chapultepec Castle and the National Museum of History

**Chapultepec Castle (Castillo de Chapultepec)** stands on a hill and is one of the city's most recognizable historical buildings. It houses the National Museum of History. According to Mexican cultural institutions, the castle has served as a military college, imperial residence, and presidential residence.

The museum galleries introduce different periods of Mexican history, while the terraces offer panoramic views of the capital. Visiting involves a climb up to the building and time to explore the exhibitions.

Inside are artworks, documents, and historic interiors. The castle's story encompasses the 19th century, the reign of Maximilian, and the country's subsequent development. Whether to choose an in-depth museum tour depends on how deeply you want to explore Mexico's history.

## The National Museum of Anthropology

Near Chapultepec stands the **[National Museum of Anthropology](/mexico/place/national-museum-of-anthropology/)**, one of the country's most important museums. Its collections explore the pre-Columbian cultures of Mesoamerica.

It is especially useful before a journey to [Teotihuacan](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/), as it helps visitors understand the historical background of the pyramids and other monuments. However, it is a separate institution with an extensive collection, not another gallery inside Chapultepec Castle.

If you want to examine both the castle and the anthropology museum in depth, avoid scheduling too many distant attractions on the same day.

## What else can you find in the park?

Chapultepec features lakes, footpaths, gardens, and various museum venues. Walking areas are spread across several sections, and moving between them takes time.

| Attraction | Reason to visit |
|---|---|
| Castle | Mexican history |
| Museum of Anthropology | Ancient cultures |
| Lakes and avenues | Walking and relaxation |
| Gardens | Plants and tranquility |

The first section is convenient for exploring the best-known attractions. Other sections differ in landscape, distances, and the kind of visit they offer. Do not assume that every section can be walked through in one short outing.

Comfortable shoes and drinking water are useful for visits to historical sites and green spaces alike. Even when much of the route is shaded, open areas can be hot.

## Planning a day in Chapultepec

For a first visit, combine two main activities: **the castle and a walk** or **the Museum of Anthropology and the park**. Either combination offers a rewarding experience while leaving time to relax.

If you want to visit several museums, check their closing days and opening hours in advance. The park being open does not mean every museum operates on the same schedule. When planning transport, identify the entrance you need because the grounds are extensive.

Architecture enthusiasts may enjoy adding a walk through central Mexico City's historic neighborhoods. However, the castle is in a different part of the city, so that combination requires a transfer.

## Why Chapultepec matters to history

Chapultepec Hill was significant even in pre-Hispanic times. Important government buildings appeared here in later centuries. This layering of history is what distinguishes the park from an ordinary urban green space.

The castle preserves material evidence of different eras, explained by the exhibitions of the National Museum of History. The large modern park around it makes it possible to combine a historical excursion with walking and relaxation.

Compared with [Templo Mayor](/mexico/place/templo-mayor/), the latter is associated with the religious life of ancient Tenochtitlan, while the castle represents later periods of Mexican history.

## Chapultepec on Ada Tours itineraries

On the [12-day Viva Mexico tour](/mexico/tour/viva-mexico/), Chapultepec is part of the capital-city section. On the [26-day journey through Central America](/multi-country/tour/central-america-8-countries-26-days/), the National Museum of Anthropology and other Mexico City monuments appear in the first few days.

These itineraries differ in scope and time allocated to museums. When choosing, check whether the program actually includes the castle or only the museum and an overview of the area. The name Chapultepec alone does not mean all attractions here are visited. You can explore the full selection in our [Mexico tour catalog](/mexico/tour/).

## Frequently asked questions about Chapultepec

### Is Chapultepec a park or a castle?

It is a large park containing a historic hilltop castle that houses the National Museum of History.

### Is the National Museum of Anthropology nearby?

Yes. The museum is beside Chapultepec Park, but it is a separate museum rather than part of the castle.

### Can I see the castle and park in one day?

Yes. This works well for a first visit if you allocate your time sensibly and choose particular sites.

### Do I need a separate museum ticket?

The castle and museums have their own admission rules. Check current tickets and opening hours before visiting.

## Tours visiting Chapultepec: how the park fits into each itinerary

[Chapultepec](/mexico/place/chapultepec/) is an extensive green area of Mexico City with avenues, lakes, and historic buildings. It contains Chapultepec Castle, home to the National Museum of History, while the [National Museum of Anthropology](/mexico/place/national-museum-of-anthropology/) is nearby. For a traveler, the area offers a chance to combine a walk and an introduction to several eras of Mexican history on the same day.

Our selection includes {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} passing through Chapultepec. These itineraries involve **an actual visit to the place**, but their programs extend far beyond the park. For an independent overview of the park, cultural attractions, and nature, see the [Chapultepec page](/mexico/place/chapultepec/). Below we explain the travel programs, excursion sequences, and the choice between a journey within Mexico and one through Central America.

## Which itineraries include Chapultepec?

### Viva Mexico: Mexico City, Oaxaca, and Yucatán

The [12-day Viva Mexico: Mexico City, Oaxaca, and Yucatán tour](/mexico/tour/viva-mexico/) begins in the capital. On day two, devoted to Mexico City's cultural heritage, Chapultepec is part of the day's geography. This capital-city section also includes the [Timeless Streets and Cultural Treasures excursion](/mexico/mexico-city-and-teotihuacan/mexico-city-history-anthropology-tour/), which introduces the historic center and the National Museum of Anthropology.

After the capital, the journey continues to [Teotihuacan](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/), then [Oaxaca](/mexico/place/oaxaca/) and the monuments of the Yucatán. This is a good choice for travelers who want to explore the history and traditions of several Mexican regions without crossing numerous international borders on a single trip.

It is important to distinguish **the places covered on a day** from the list of specific admission tickets. Chapultepec is named in the itinerary, but a full tour of the castle and National Museum of History must not automatically be assumed to be included. Check the day's schedule and conditions if that visit is important to you.

### Central America: Eight Countries in 26 Days

On the [Central America: Eight Countries in 26 Days itinerary](/multi-country/tour/central-america-8-countries-26-days/), Chapultepec is also visited near the beginning, on day two in Mexico City. The sightseeing tour combines the [Zócalo](/mexico/place/mexico-city-zocalo/), the cathedral, Templo Mayor, Chapultepec, and the [National Museum of Anthropology](/mexico/place/national-museum-of-anthropology/). This part of the program has its own [Mexico City: Zócalo, Chapultepec, and Anthropology Museum excursion](/mexico/mexico-city-and-teotihuacan/mexico-city-zocalo-chapultepec-anthropology/).

The route then continues to [Teotihuacan](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/), the Yucatán, Belize, Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and Panama. Chapultepec is among the first cultural experiences before the extended journey. Visiting it does not turn the entire trip into a tour of Mexico City.

For this option, the most important considerations are the time available, documentation for crossing borders, and readiness for frequent travel. It is a much longer journey than the 12-day Mexico program.

## Comparing the two routes

| Question | Difference |
|---|---|
| Geography | Mexico only or eight countries |
| Chapultepec | Near the start of both tours |
| What comes next | Oaxaca and Yucatán or Central America |
| Pace | Several regions of one country or a long international route |

Both itineraries offer an opportunity to see Chapultepec, but their goals differ. If Mexican crafts, historical towns, and Maya archaeology interest you, it makes sense to start with [Viva Mexico](/mexico/tour/viva-mexico/). If you want to combine a cultural day in Mexico City with volcanoes, forests, and towns elsewhere in the region, compare the full [26-day journey](/multi-country/tour/central-america-8-countries-26-days/).

For other ways to discover the capital, see [Mexico tours](/mexico/tour/) and [Mexico City excursions](/mexico/mexico-city-and-teotihuacan/). These neighboring collections serve different purposes: one covers all trips in the country, and the other focuses on excursions, whereas this page features only routes that include Chapultepec as a main stop.

## What exactly should you see in Chapultepec?

Chapultepec combines parkland and museums. The hilltop castle preserves evidence of several historical periods, including the viceregal era, the Second Mexican Empire, and the country's later history. It now houses the National Museum of History. Its official exhibitions cover Mexican history from the Spanish conquest to the revolution.

The National Museum of Anthropology, also in this part of the city, focuses on the cultures of precolonial Mexico. It provides context for monuments found later in the journey: [Teotihuacan](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/), [Uxmal](/mexico/place/uxmal/), and [Chichén Itzá](/mexico/place/chichen-itza/).

However, **the park, castle, and Museum of Anthropology are separate attractions**. A day described as a sightseeing tour does not automatically include every hall in both museums. The duration of the excursion, opening hours, and ticket arrangements determine what can actually be covered. Admission to the National Museum of History is especially important to arrange separately if it is not listed in your program.

## How much time to allow and how to prepare

A few hours can be enough to walk the avenues and see some nearby attractions. Exploring the Museum of Anthropology and the castle thoroughly takes substantially longer. When Chapultepec is part of a sightseeing day with the Zócalo and Templo Mayor, focus on **the stops actually listed**; a full museum visit will not fit into every short city tour.

Mexico City sits at a high elevation. Mornings and evenings can feel cooler than on the Yucatán coast. Comfortable shoes are useful both in the park and on city walks. Check museum hours and possible closure days just before your trip, as schedules can change.

If Chapultepec is your main priority in the capital, consider adding free time in Mexico City. This lets you enjoy the castle, anthropology museum, or a walk through the park without trying to see everything during the shared sightseeing day.

## Frequently asked questions about tours through Chapultepec

### On which day is Chapultepec visited?

On both itineraries discussed here, the park appears on day two, during the capital-city section. The order of individual stops within that day is specified in the relevant itinerary and excursion module.

### Is Chapultepec Castle included in both tours?

Chapultepec itself is listed in the geography of both journeys, but this does not confirm admission to the National Museum of History inside the castle. To visit it, look for a specific mention of the museum and admission ticket in the terms.

### Can I visit Chapultepec and the National Museum of Anthropology together?

Yes, the attractions are close to each other. On the [26-day route](/multi-country/tour/central-america-8-countries-26-days/), Chapultepec and the anthropology museum are part of the same sightseeing day. However, the depth of the visit depends on the excursion time. Allow additional time if you want to explore the museum collection thoroughly.

### Do I need a long tour just to see one park?

No. The international journey makes sense if you want to visit all eight countries. For Chapultepec alone, a stay in Mexico City with an appropriate excursion or free time is sufficient. Start with [Mexico City excursions](/mexico/mexico-city-and-teotihuacan/) and the [park's own page](/mexico/place/chapultepec/).

### Which itinerary is better for Mexican history?

If you want to explore Mexico itself in more depth, including museums, Oaxaca, and the Yucatán, choose [Viva Mexico](/mexico/tour/viva-mexico/). If a cultural day in Mexico City should be the start of a wider Central American journey, the [26-day itinerary](/multi-country/tour/central-america-8-countries-26-days/) is more suitable.

## Chichén Itzá: what to see in the ancient Maya city

Chichén Itzá is one of the most important archaeological complexes on Mexico's [Yucatán Peninsula](/mexico/). Its surviving structures include pyramids, temples, courts for ritual ball games, and buildings associated with observations of the sky. Chichén Itzá is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and its monuments show the interaction of Maya architectural traditions with influences from central Mexico.

Allow several hours for the archaeological zone itself, plus travel time. If your journey begins on the Caribbean coast, a visit to Chichén Itzá will take a dedicated excursion day.

## El Castillo: the Pyramid of Kukulcán

The complex's best-known building is **El Castillo**, or the Temple of Kukulcán. This stepped pyramid rises above a vast open plaza. Its stairways and carefully organized facades reveal the connection between the ancient city's architecture, religious beliefs, and calendar observations.

View the pyramid from permitted paths. Climbing vulnerable ancient structures may be prohibited, and a beautiful photograph is not permission to climb. Photography and visitor behavior are governed by the archaeological site's INAH regulations.

## Temple of the Warriors, columns, and the ball court

The northern part of Chichén Itzá contains the **Temple of the Warriors** and the **Group of a Thousand Columns**. These ensembles convey the scale of the ceremonial space and the complexity of its stone architecture. Preserved reliefs, columns, and the spaces around the plazas are as important as the large stairways.

The **Great Ball Court** is an attraction in its own right. The game had ritual significance in Mesoamerican cultures. The court is striking for the length of its walls and stone carvings. Give it a dedicated stop instead of treating it as an afterthought to a photograph of El Castillo.

Another famous structure is **El Caracol**, a circular building commonly associated with astronomical observations. Its form differs markedly from the stepped temples.

## Cenotes, water, and the city's history

Ancient settlements on the Yucatán depended on underground water sources. The name Chichén Itzá itself is connected with the region's natural limestone sinkholes, or cenotes, which had both practical and religious significance. The natural geography of the complex helps explain why a city developed here.

Travelers often arrange a separate visit to a nearby cenote, such as Ik Kil. A cultural excursion among the monuments and a swim in a separate pool are different experiences, potentially with different tickets, opening hours, and regulations.

## Getting here from Cancún or Mérida

[Cancún](/mexico/place/cancun/) on the Caribbean coast and [Mérida](/mexico/place/merida/) inland on the Yucatán are convenient starting points for Chichén Itzá. Driving across the peninsula takes time, so allow a full day for a trip from Cancún, including the transfer and sightseeing.

If your journey also includes [Tulum](/mexico/place/tulum/) or [Cobá](/mexico/place/coba/), remember that these are separate archaeological sites. They differ in historical context, location, and access conditions. Trying to visit all the monuments in one day without planning the logistics would be inconvenient.

## How to allocate your time on site

| Stage | Main interest |
|---|---|
| First plazas | El Castillo |
| Northern complex | Temple of the Warriors |
| Separate walk | The ball court |
| Another area of the site | El Caracol |

Mentioning individual monuments does not guarantee access inside every building. Check current INAH routes and archaeological-zone operating arrangements before your visit. The official resource also provides information on separate payments, including a state-level Yucatán fee; exact amounts and visitor categories should be checked for your travel date.

Bring water, comfortable shoes for a long walk, sun protection, and time to rest. The heat in open plazas can feel stronger than in a city's shaded streets.

## Which tour combines Chichén Itzá with the coast?

Our [Mexico travel catalog](/mexico/tour/) includes cultural programs and routes that continue to the coast. For example, the [eight-day Mexico Lindo tour](/mexico/tour/mexico-lindo-eight-days/) includes Chichén Itzá in its main itinerary, followed by the Caribbean coast.

For ancient cities and museums, explore [Culture and History](/interests/culture-and-history/). When choosing a route, examine the actual days, transfer conditions, and admission tickets included in your specific tour.

## Frequently asked questions about Chichén Itzá

### Is Chichén Itzá a Maya site?

Yes. It is an important center of Maya civilization, and its monuments also reflect historical influences from other Mesoamerican traditions.

### Can I climb the Pyramid of Kukulcán?

Visitors must follow current INAH restrictions. Do not count on climbing the pyramid: sightseeing takes place on permitted paths and viewing areas.

### Can I visit Chichén Itzá from Cancún in one day?

Yes, but it is a full excursion day that includes the road journey, time to explore the site, and the return trip.

## What happens on a day at Chichén Itzá?

The complex is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Alongside El Castillo, it includes the Temple of the Warriors, the large ritual ball court, and other stone buildings. The [Chichén Itzá page](/mexico/place/chichen-itza/) describes the site in more detail; when selecting a tour, what matters most is how much sightseeing time is allocated and whether a guide is included.

The [six-day Mexico City–Mérida–Cancún tour](/mexico/tour/mexico-city-merida-uxmal-kabah-chichen-itza/) specifies a local English- and Spanish-speaking guide, an admission ticket, and a transfer to a coastal hotel. These terms apply to that particular itinerary. Other routes may differ in guiding language, included tickets, and the order of stops. Read the excursion description alongside the “Included” section.

## Ik Kil Cenote, Valladolid, and the coast

On the [Cancún–Belize journey](/multi-country/tour/cancun-belize-11-days/), the Chichén Itzá day ends with swimming in [Ik Kil Cenote](/mexico/place/ik-kil-cenote/). A similar progression from archaeology to nature appears on the [route via Tulum and Palenque](/mexico/tour/mexico-cancun-tulum-palenque-uxmal-chichen-itza/). On [Mexico Lindo](/mexico/tour/mexico-lindo-eight-days/), Chichén Itzá and the cenote are joined by a stop in [Valladolid](/mexico/place/valladolid/), after which the group continues to the [Riviera Maya](/mexico/place/riviera-maya/).

Not all cenotes are equally easy places to swim: access steps, equipment, and visitor numbers vary. Nor should the name of a stop alone be taken to mean the admission ticket, lunch, or equipment hire is included. Check the specific itinerary.

Another route might combine the Yucatán with sites such as [Uxmal](/mexico/place/uxmal/), [Kabah](/mexico/place/kabah/), or [Tulum](/mexico/place/tulum/). Pay attention to which days these visits fall on so that there is enough time for each complex.

## From Mexico City or Cancún: which starting point is better?

**Starting in Mexico City** generally makes sense if you want to discover several historic regions. The [Grand Mexican Holiday](/mexico/tour/grand-mexico-holiday/) goes through the capital, Chiapas, Campeche, and Yucatán. [Viva Mexico](/mexico/tour/viva-mexico/) adds Oaxaca. These programs involve more transfers but offer a broader picture of the country.

**Starting in Cancún** is convenient for a journey combining Maya monuments and the Caribbean. On the [11-day Cancún and Belize tour](/multi-country/tour/cancun-belize-11-days/), day two features Chichén Itzá and a cenote, and day three features [Tulum](/mexico/place/tulum/) and [Cobá](/mexico/place/coba/). The route later continues in Belize. This is a two-country journey with separate flight and entry requirements.

The [Mexico gastronomy tour](/mexico/tour/mexico-gourmet-discovery-2024/) explores the Yucatán alongside markets, local cuisine, cenotes, and other attractions. It suits travelers who want to complement archaeology with Mexican food culture.

## How much travel time should you allow?

The [Mexico City–Mérida–Chichén Itzá itinerary](/mexico/tour/mexico-city-merida-uxmal-kabah-chichen-itza/) gives approximately two hours from Mérida to the archaeological zone and around three hours onward to Cancún. These are estimates for that particular route; hotels, traffic, and stops can affect actual durations.

When planning the excursion day, allow separately for the journey to the complex, sightseeing, and the next transfer. Adding a cenote or Valladolid makes the day more full. INAH tickets and regional fees are practical visitor considerations; their scope and cost should be checked before traveling. Follow the selected itinerary for the terms of services already paid for.

## Chichén Itzá on a longer journey around Central America

On the [Central America: Eight Countries in 26 Days tour](/multi-country/tour/central-america-8-countries-26-days/), Chichén Itzá appears on the Mexican leg before the route reaches Cancún and continues into Belize. Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and Panama follow. This option is designed to explore a large region, so international travel and changing climate zones occupy a substantial part of the time.

If your main goal is Yucatán archaeology, a shorter itinerary may leave more time for [Chichén Itzá](/mexico/place/chichen-itza/), [Uxmal](/mexico/place/uxmal/), and surrounding towns. Choose an international journey for all the countries it covers rather than for just one excursion.

## Questions about tours via Chichén Itzá

### Can I combine Chichén Itzá and a cenote on the same day?

Yes. Several itineraries explicitly include that sequence, such as the [Cancún–Belize tour](/multi-country/tour/cancun-belize-11-days/). Swimming time and specific services depend on the selected route.

### Do all programs include a Russian-speaking guide?

No. Some excursions list local English- and Spanish-speaking guides, while others specify Russian-speaking accompaniment. Check the language in the individual tour, not in the general collection.

### Which is a better starting point: Mérida or Cancún?

[Mérida](/mexico/place/merida/) is convenient for exploring Yucatán's archaeological monuments, while [Cancún](/mexico/place/cancun/) is better suited to a trip with a beach holiday. The decision depends on the full sequence of days and where the journey ends.

### Is there a separate short tour exclusively to Chichén Itzá?

This selection contains routes with an obligatory visit to Chichén Itzá. You can discuss a shorter private trip separately; the collection itself does not confirm that a dedicated ready-made itinerary exists or what it costs.

## Cholula in Mexico: the Great Pyramid and a city below the volcanoes

Cholula lies near [Puebla](/mexico/place/puebla/) in central [Mexico](/mexico/). The city is famous for its archaeological complex with a huge pyramid crowned by a Catholic church built in colonial times. Everyday life continues all around: cafés and shops are open, families celebrate special occasions, and streets connect old squares with residential neighborhoods.

What makes Cholula particularly interesting is the contrast between eras. Here an ancient structure can look like a green hill topped by the silhouette of a church. When exploring its history, remember that the pyramid and church belong to different periods.

## The Great Pyramid of Cholula: why it is unusual

The archaeological complex contains **the Great Pyramid of Cholula**, built and modified over a long period. Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) describes it as the pyramid with the largest base area in Mesoamerica, approximately 450 meters along each side.

It looks very different from the exposed stone steps of Chichén Itzá: much of the ancient structure lies hidden beneath soil and later construction. This is why historical explanations matter during a visit; without them, the pyramid could easily be mistaken for a natural hill.

On top stands the **Sanctuary of Our Lady of Remedies** (Nuestra Señora de los Remedios). The pairing of an ancient pyramid and a Catholic church shows how the region's cultural landscape has changed.

## What can be visited in the archaeological zone?

Cholula's archaeological zone includes accessible outdoor areas and a museum exhibition. INAH also describes a system of internal tunnels, but its official website notes that **the underground route is closed until further notice**.

Plan your visit around the permitted outdoor areas, museum, and views of the complex rather than expecting to walk through the pyramid's tunnels. Access to individual sections and visitor regulations may change.

In the open-air areas, look at the surviving archaeological remains, the arrangement of ceremonial courtyards, and the hill's overall appearance. Their significance differs from the later urban architecture around the church.

## Cholula's historic neighborhoods and volcanic skyline

After exploring the archaeological site, take a walk through the town center. Colorful facades, churches, small squares, and ordinary city streets alternate along the way. This transition from a major monument to the surrounding neighborhoods makes a visit varied and rewarding.

On clear days, the region offers views of **Popocatépetl** and **Iztaccíhuatl** volcanoes. They form a distant mountain backdrop, but visibility depends on cloud cover and atmospheric conditions. A visit to the city is not an excursion up an active volcano; access to volcanic zones is governed separately.

## Cholula and Puebla in one day

Cholula and [Puebla](/mexico/place/puebla/) played different historical roles. Puebla is particularly known for colonial architecture, tile-covered facades, and urban churches. Cholula adds an introduction to earlier Mesoamerican history.

| Stop | What to see |
|---|---|
| Cholula | Pyramid and church |
| Puebla | Cathedral and historic neighborhoods |

Allow a full day for both places, and more time if you are interested in museums and unhurried walks. As visits to the archaeological zone involve walking through open areas, bring comfortable shoes, water, and sun protection.

## How Cholula differs from Teotihuacan

[Teotihuacan](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/) is famous for its Pyramids of the Sun and Moon and the long ceremonial avenue. Cholula's defining monument is a layered pyramid topped by a colonial church. Despite the shared word “pyramid,” the sites differ in architecture, historical development, and context.

On an itinerary through central Mexico, they represent distinct days and different excursion themes. Choose priorities according to actual travel time rather than the number of attractions listed.

## When to visit and how to prepare

Cholula lies in Mexico's highlands. Days can be sunny, with temperatures falling toward evening. Check the forecast, archaeological-zone access, and museum opening hours. During major celebrations, the church area and central streets may have additional restrictions or large crowds.

## Frequently asked questions about Cholula

### Is Cholula's pyramid larger than other pyramids in Mexico?

INAH particularly highlights its base area. Comparing the “size” of different pyramids without specifying height and volume is misleading.

### Are the tunnels inside the pyramid open?

The official INAH page lists access to the tunnels as closed until further notice. Check for updates before your trip.

### Can I combine Cholula with Puebla?

Yes. These cities are near each other, making it convenient to combine a pre-Columbian monument with Puebla's colonial neighborhoods on the same itinerary.
